accepted_phrases: Arrow keys serve real navigation functions and software can remap functional layouts. The K12 exposes arrows through Fn combinations, while the K6 explicitly supplies dedicated arrows. One long-term HHKB owner reports that layered arrows became natural muscle memory, while another buyer rejects 60 percent specifically to retain arrows. Because this commuter prioritizes direct arrows and modifier shortcuts, the K6 fits the stated workflow unless a hands-on K12 trial changes that preference.

The K12 and MX Keys Mini runtime statements depend on backlight conditions, and the K6 body contains materially different up-to-10-hour, up-to-72-hour, and nine-normal-use-day statements. The Corne discussion shows large effects from display, LED, battery and configuration choices, but its custom-build anecdotes cannot predict any candidate. All three product runtimes remain conditional seller claims rather than observed commute endurance.

Bluetooth is a short-range low-power wire-replacement protocol used for keyboard communication, but neither that generic description nor any frozen product body measures product-specific end-to-end latency or perceptibility. Bluetooth 5.1 and Low Energy labels do not prove imperceptible lag. K12 and K6 explicitly provide wired keyboard input as a fallback, while the MX Keys Mini body's USB-C rechargeable wording is not evidence of wired input.

The frozen K12 is $99.99 with no reviews, a 60 percent 61-key layout, Fn-layer arrows, Bluetooth 5.1, wired Type-C input and a conditional 240-hour claim. The K6 is $83.99 with no reviews, a 65 percent 68-key layout, dedicated arrows, Bluetooth 5.1, wired Type-C input, 317 by 107 by 37 millimetre dimensions, 2.25-pound weight and internally different conditional runtime statements. The MX Keys Mini is $99.99 with 52/100 from 12 reviews, Bluetooth Low Energy, a thinner and lighter profile and a conditional 10-day or five-month claim, but no stated wired keyboard input. None supplies measured Bluetooth typing latency.

Use stated product dimensions and weight only when the product body identifies them, and do not substitute package dimensions. A different owner's report that a heavy Feker Alice 80 was nonportable, hard to fit in a case and dependent on a manual for secondary functions shows why physical and functional fit need testing, but it does not measure any candidate. A bag, table, shortcut and carrying-comfort trial remains required.

I recommend the Keychron K6 dedicated-arrow wired-fallback route for this commuter because its frozen body combines a compact 65 percent layout, dedicated arrows, explicit Bluetooth and wired input, three-device switching, stated dimensions and a rechargeable battery. I preserve its 2.25-pound weight, no-review display, conflicting conditional runtime wording, wireless 6KRO boundary and absent measured Bluetooth latency. I would carry its cable, test it in the actual bag and table, and defer if its weight or shortcut placement fails that trial.
I recommend the Keychron K6 dedicated-arrow wired-fallback route.
Choose the Keychron K6 route, subject to a physical fit trial and preserved battery and latency uncertainty.
The frozen K12 body states that it has four dedicated arrow keys.
Owner reports prove that Fn-layer arrows are unusable for everyone.
The K6 is guaranteed to last nine workdays on every charge under all settings.
The Corne thread proves that the K6 battery will last either less than one day or roughly two months.
Bluetooth 5.1 proves that the K6 and K12 have imperceptible end-to-end typing latency.
The MX Keys Mini USB-C rechargeable wording proves that the cable carries wired keyboard input.
The Feker Alice 80 owner report proves that the Keychron K6 cannot fit in a commuter bag.

research_subgoals.description: Build a complete frozen matrix for K12, K6 and MX Keys Mini, including price, review display, layout, arrow access, connectivity, device switching, battery wording, dimensions, weight, rollover and absent measured latency.
Reconcile arrow-key functions, software remapping, opposing owner preferences and the K12 versus K6 physical access methods under this commuter's shortcut habits.
Audit every conditional battery statement, preserve the K6 internal discrepancy, and use Corne anecdotes only to explain implementation sensitivity rather than transfer runtime numbers.
Explain Bluetooth's generic keyboard-link role, identify the missing product-specific latency and perceptibility measurements, and distinguish wired input from USB-C charging wording.
Use stated product measurements and the scoped Feker portability counterexample to define a real bag, table, shortcut and carrying-comfort trial without transferring another model's outcome.
Apply all verified branches to one commuter route or a defer decision while preserving every seller, owner, battery, weight, fit, wired-input and latency limitation.

query_requirements.text: Audit all three complete frozen product bodies for exact price, review display, layout, arrow access, Bluetooth and wired-input wording, device switching, conditional battery statements, dimensions, weight, rollover and absent measured latency.
Explain arrow-key functions and functional remapping, reconcile the long-term layered-arrow experience with the dedicated-arrow preference, and apply the result to this commuter's modifier shortcuts.
Preserve backlight and usage conditions for every seller runtime, surface the K6 internal discrepancy, and scope the custom Corne battery reports without transferring their numbers.
Separate generic Bluetooth mechanisms and version labels from product-specific measured or perceptible typing latency, and do not promote USB-C charging to wired keyboard input.
Audit physical commute fit using stated product measurements and a scoped portability counterexample, then require a real bag, table, shortcut and carrying-comfort trial.
Recommend one route or defer under the compact-fit, dedicated-arrow, shortcut, wired-fallback and evidence-scope constraints, preserving every uncertainty and stating the practical carry plan.
